metaDescription: Five tent heaters under $100, led by a two-setting radiant propane heater approved for ventilated indoor use, with CO and ventilation rules for winter camping.
expertTake: The Mr. Heater Portable Buddy is the best tent heater here because it is approved for indoor and outdoor use, has two heat settings and carries a documented safety design. The BEYOND HEAT milkhouse unit is the best pick on a powered site. Anyone tempted to run a fuel heater overnight in a sealed tent should not buy a heater at all. Whatever you buy, practise lighting it at home and bring a working alarm. Add a small thermometer to the tent so you can turn the heater down as soon as the space is comfortable.
introParagraphs: A hundred dollars buys the first heaters that were designed with enclosed use in mind. They add sensing and shutoff hardware that cheaper units skip, which is exactly the part that matters in a small fabric room.
Even so, ventilation, a carbon monoxide alarm and clearance from fabric remain your responsibility. The $100 cap reflects listing prices on the date this guide was updated, and prices move.

products.name: Mr. Heater 9,000 BTU Portable Buddy radiant propane heater

specList.label: Approval
specList.value: Designed and approved for indoor and outdoor use

specList.label: Safety
specList.value: Oxygen sensor and tip-over shutoff (maker design)

products.description:
The Portable Buddy emits either 4,000 or 9,000 BTU per hour of radiant heat, and the listing says it is designed and approved for indoor and outdoor use and heats roughly 225 square feet. The two settings are the key advantage: the 4,000 BTU step suits a small tent, and the 9,000 BTU step is for a large shelter or a cold start. Mr. Heater builds it with an oxygen depletion sensor and tip-over shutoff.

It is a radiant design that warms objects and people, not the whole volume of air, so a tent warms unevenly and you feel it most in front of the heater. Compared with the Little Buddy at 3,800 BTU, it is stronger and more flexible. Compared with the CAMPLUX it is heavier but better documented.

Ventilation is still required, so open two vents, keep a battery carbon monoxide alarm at head height and keep the heater clear of fabric. Check hose and cylinder connections with soapy water, use the lower step in a tent, and switch it off before sleeping. Use the low step as your default and treat the high step as a ten-minute boost.
products.bestFor: Medium tents and shelters with ventilation.
pros: Approved for indoor and outdoor use
cons: Still burns fuel, so ventilation is required
9,000 BTU is too much for a small tent

products.name: CAMPLUX 8,500 BTU portable propane heater, tilt switch, tripod base
products.description:
The CAMPLUX is an 8,500 BTU propane heater with two heat speeds, a safety tilt switch that shuts it off if it tips and a detachable tripod base for uneven ground. At 4.2 pounds it is light enough to carry on a camping trip. The listing positions it as an outdoor and patio heater, with dual safety protection.

Compared with the Portable Buddy, it is lighter and has a tripod, but the listing gives less indoor approval detail. In a tent, that matters. Treat it as an outdoor and vestibule heater unless the manual says otherwise.

Keep it three feet from fabric, always ventilate and carry a CO alarm. In practice, set it on a board, light it with the tent door open and let it run for ten minutes before closing vents to a gap. Keep the alarm testing habit, because it is the only thing that tells you the air has gone wrong. Pick up the heater only when it is cold, and let the cylinder cool before packing.

products.name: BEYOND HEAT 1500W milkhouse heater with thermostat
products.description:
The BEYOND HEAT is a milkhouse-style metal fan heater with a thermostat, fan-only mode, a lower step and a tip-over switch. It makes no combustion gases, which makes it the safest choice with power.

It draws 12.5 amps at 1500 watts, so use a short heavy cord and a dedicated circuit. Compared with the Portable Buddy, it cannot work off grid but removes the CO risk.

Keep it on a flat board and clear of fabric. If you choose this one, build the layout around the heater: put it off the walkway, keep pets and children away and make sure nothing hangs over it. The thermostat cycles the element, so you hear the fan stop and start through the night, which is normal. Owners like the quiet hum of a thermostat-cycled fan better than the hiss of a gas burner, and they like not worrying about a detector going off at 3 a.m. The cost is a cord and a campsite with power. Keep the unit off the groundsheet's wet patches and run the cord out of the door in a drip loop.

products.name: Buyplus 10,000 BTU single-tank-top propane heater
products.description:
The Buyplus is a tank-top propane heater with a steel body and mesh guard. Its title claims 10,000 BTU.

It is top-heavy and strong, suited to large shelters and outdoor use, not small tents.

Use it with ventilation and a CO alarm. Because the tank threads onto the top, a bump to the heater tips the whole assembly, so place it on a board where nobody walks. It suits a large screened shelter far more than a sleeping tent. Compared with the Portable Buddy it has no stated indoor approval and no variable output, so every decision falls on you. Cold air also makes the regulator behave differently, so test it at home in the cold before relying on it in the field. Wind and moisture are bigger enemies than temperature for this style, so keep the regulator dry and the burner out of drafts.

products.name: Mr. Heater Little Buddy 3,800 BTU radiant propane heater
products.description:
The Little Buddy is a 3,800 BTU radiant propane heater with one-button ignition and a compact base. It is the right size for a small tent.

It uses one pound cylinders, which run out fast.

Ventilate and use an alarm. Switching to a hose and a larger cylinder brings cost per hour down, and Mr. Heater sells an adapter hose. Store one pound cylinders upright and away from heat, and never refill disposable ones. In use, it is a tent heater for one or two people. Start it outside the tent or at the door, move it in once the flame is steady, and keep it at floor level on a board. Replace the cylinder in the open air, away from any flame or spark.
cons: One pound cylinders run out fast

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Portable Buddy is listed as designed and approved for indoor and outdoor use. Many cheaper heaters do not say so. In a tent that difference is a safety feature. For a family cabin tent of 100 square feet or more, the 9,000 BTU step of the Portable Buddy is useful for the first twenty minutes, then drop to 4,000. A quick sizing guide is to match 30 to 40 BTU per square foot for light camping heat, so a 60 square foot tent needs only a couple of thousand BTU for comfort, and anything more is overkill. Plan where the cold air enters: a door vent low and a roof vent high lets fresh air sweep through as the heater runs.

The Portable Buddy offers 4,000 and 9,000 BTU, and the CAMPLUX has two speeds. A low setting avoids overheating a small tent and saves fuel. A tent warms unevenly with radiant heat, so place the heater where people sit, not where they sleep. Look for a heater whose manual explicitly mentions tents, since a manual that bans enclosed use is a clear answer. Check that your sleeping area is far enough from the heater that a rolled bag or a boot cannot touch it.

Every fuel heater here needs two vents and a battery CO alarm. Electric units like the BEYOND HEAT avoid the issue entirely. Use two vents at different heights, because warm air rises and fresh air sinks. Use a hose and bulk cylinder where possible, because one pound cylinders add cost and waste.

The CAMPLUX weighs 4.2 lb and has a tripod, while the Buyplus is top-heavy. Use a flat board on soft ground. Check the cylinder seat for debris before each connection, because a poor seal is the usual leak. Know your tent: a double-wall tent with a rainfly traps heat better than a single-wall shelter, which affects how much heater you need.

A one pound cylinder on the Little Buddy lasts a few hours. A hose to a larger tank saves money and trips. Do not hang wet clothes near a heater, which is both a fire and a moisture issue. Keep spare, fresh batteries for the alarm and put it where you sleep, not next to the heater.

A 1500W heater draws 12.5 amps. Use a short heavy cord and a dedicated circuit. Stop using the heater and ventilate if the alarm sounds, you feel dizzy or the flame turns yellow. Learn the shut-off steps in daylight, so you can do it half-asleep and in the dark. If you are unsure between two heaters, choose the one whose manual you can actually understand.

specDecoder.meaning: The maker states the heater meets standards for enclosed spaces with ventilation. It matters most in a tent.
Heat that warms objects and people directly. Radiant heat falls with distance.
A switch that cuts gas on tipping. It stops gas if the heater leans.
Heat per hour. Choose by tent volume.
A rugged metal fan heater. It is a tough fan unit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Enclosed-use approval
howWeEvaluated.description: We scored stated approvals. The Portable Buddy led. Approval statements were weighed against what the manual would actually say. Approval wording was read closely, because 'outdoor and patio' and 'indoor approved' are very different claims.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat settings
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared steps and outputs. Weight was compared with the carry distance a camper expects. The cost per hour of the fuel was noted as a practical factor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety hardware
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted sensors and tilt switches. Sensing hardware counted higher than marketing words. Whether a listing mentions tents specifically was counted as a plus.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and stability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared bases and carry weight. Stability on soft ground was considered. Wind exposure of open burners was considered.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on spec sheets and listing feedback patterns, we weighed reports of tipping and leaks. Reports of ignition trouble in the cold were noted. We also considered how easy each unit is to light and shut off in the dark. Final scores leaned toward the units that tell you exactly what they are built to do.

howToChoose.note: Measure the tent and note the lowest expected temperature before you shop.
Prices move, so read the tiers as relative positions. Check the listing again before ordering, since prices and stock change quickly in camping season.

cards.label: Fuel

howToChoose.note: Choose electric if you have power. For most campers the real choice is electric if there is a hookup, otherwise the approved radiant unit. If your trip is a single weekend, rent or borrow before you buy.
On uneven ground, a flat board and a tripod matter more than extra BTU.

cards.text: Approval, two settings and sensing hardware.

howToChoose.note: Layers and a pad beat any heater.

howToChoose.note: Spending more buys approvals and sensing, which are what you want in a small fabric room.

maintenance.why: Gas leaks are the biggest risk. Skipping this is how a small leak goes unnoticed on a trip. Do it with soapy water and no flame nearby.
A dead alarm protects nobody. Replace batteries every season. Replace the battery at the start of each season.
Debris cuts output. A clean burner has an even flame. Brush off dust, especially around the sensor and pilot area.
A hot plug signals a poor connection. A hot plug is a reason to stop using the heater. Check the whole length of the cord.
Moisture damages igniters. Dry storage prevents rust. Pack with silica gel in a dry box.

faq.q: Is the Portable Buddy tent safe?
faq.a: It is approved for indoor use with ventilation, but you still need two vents and a CO alarm. Approved for indoor use does not mean approved for sleeping with it on, and the manual will say so.
The low step in a tent. A CO alarm is cheap insurance and should be a battery model rated for portable use.
Yes, it makes no combustion gases. If you want zero risk of fumes, buy electric and camp where there is power.

faq.q: Can I sleep with it on?
faq.a: No. Cylinders last longer on the low step, and a bulk tank through a hose lowers the cost per hour.

faq.q: How long does a cylinder last?
faq.a: A one pound cylinder lasts a few hours. If wind picks up, stop and shelter the heater, because a gust can blow out a flame. If the flame looks yellow, shut it off and get fresh air, because a yellow flame means poor combustion.

Shield open burners from gusts. Cold weather also drains batteries, so keep spare alarm batteries warm in a pocket. Keep children out of the heater's reach and never use it to dry boots. Practise lighting and shutting off the heater at home first, so the field routine is automatic.
